failing_part: "a standard regression that adjusts for the confounder at every time point gives an unbiased estimate of the total effect ... MSMs are needed only to gain efficiency"
narrowest_regime: Nowhere in the stated regime. Conditional regression is unbiased for the total effect only when no time-varying confounder is affected by earlier exposure (or there is no confounding by it at all), which is outside the stated regime.
reason: When L_t is both a confounder of later exposure and a consequence of earlier exposure, adjusting for it blocks the part of the earlier exposure's effect mediated through L_t and, if L_t shares an unmeasured cause with the outcome, opens a collider path; not adjusting leaves confounding. Standard regression is therefore biased whether or not it adjusts, which is exactly the problem MSMs (IPTW), the g-formula and g-estimation solve. The cited paper's abstract states the opposite of the claim: 'standard approaches for adjustment of confounding are biased when there exist time-dependent confounders that are also affected by previous treatment.'

citations.cite: Robins JM, Hernán MA, Brumback B. Marginal structural models and causal inference in epidemiology. Epidemiology 2000;11(5):550-560 (abstract retrieved via PubMed E-utilities, PMID 10955408)
Hernán MA, Robins JM. Causal Inference: What If. Chapman & Hall/CRC 2020, ch. 20 (treatment-confounder feedback)

bite_note: Acting on it would steer a researcher to conditional regression instead of IPTW/g-formula/g-estimation, giving a biased total-effect estimate; it inverts the method recommendation.

failing_part: "the ordinary paired t on rK − 1 = 49 degrees of freedom ... gives an approximately valid 95% interval, because repeating the folds 10 times makes the fold differences approximately independent"
narrowest_regime: Nowhere on a 10×5 repeated CV substrate. The 50 differences share training rows (overlap 3/4 within a repeat) and the same 200-or-whatever data rows across repeats; a valid interval needs the Nadeau–Bengio corrected variance (1/(rK) + n_test/n_train)·s², i.e. Bouckaert & Frank's corrected repeated k-fold t, or a different design (5×2 cv, outer bootstrap).
reason: Repeating the folds does not make the differences independent: each repeat reuses the same observations, so the 50 differences are strongly positively correlated, s²_d/(rK) badly underestimates the variance of mean(d), and the effective df is far below 49. My simulation of two symmetric OLS models (equal true performance, n=200, 10×5 CV, 400 data sets) gave a 60.0% rejection rate for the naive t at nominal 5%, against 4.8% for the Nadeau–Bengio corrected t. The cited sources say the opposite: Dietterich 1998 found the k-fold CV paired t has elevated Type I error, and Bouckaert & Frank 2004 showed that the uncorrected repeated-CV t is the worst offender and proposed the corrected repeated k-fold test.

citations.cite: Dietterich TG. Approximate statistical tests for comparing supervised classification learning algorithms. Neural Computation 1998;10(7):1895-1923 (metadata via Crossref)
Bouckaert RR, Frank E. Evaluating the replicability of significance tests for comparing learning algorithms. PAKDD 2004, LNCS 3056:3-12 (metadata via Crossref)
Nadeau C, Bengio Y. Inference for the generalization error. Machine Learning 2003;52:239-281 (metadata via Crossref)

bite_note: The interval comes out far too narrow (about 60% false 'differences' when two families are truly equal), so a researcher would wrongly declare one family better. The corrected variance would widen it by roughly sqrt(1 + rK·n_test/n_train) ≈ 3.7× at 10×5.

failing_part: "coding it as one indicator or as a numeric amount gives the same slope, interval ... (only the intercept's reference changes)"
narrowest_regime: Unpenalized GLMs with an intercept, or tree models: predictions, fit and the predictor's test statistic/p-value are identical under either coding for any two values a<b. The slope and its interval are also identical only when b − a = 1 and the indicator marks the larger value (e.g. 0/1, 1/2 codings). Penalized fits are invariant only if the predictor is standardized first.
reason: With values a and b, x = a + (b−a)·I, so the coding change is affine. The fitted values and the t statistic are unchanged, but the slope on x equals the slope on I divided by (b−a), and so does its interval; the intercept is not the only thing that moves. If the 'yes' level is the smaller value, the sign flips too. My check (values 0/2) gave slope 0.389 [0.268, 0.509] as an amount versus 0.778 [0.536, 1.019] as an indicator, with identical t = 6.35 and predictions identical to 1e-15. An unstandardized ridge fit's predictions differed by up to 0.13. The imputation-model part is an assertion about the app's code that I could not and did not check.
bite_note: The decision not to ask is harmless for predictions and p-values, but for any two-valued column whose gap is not 1 (0/2, −1/1, 1/3, a 0/100 mg dose) the reported 'slope' is the group contrast divided by the gap. A researcher reading it as the yes-vs-no difference would be off by that factor. Penalized fits on unstandardized inputs also change their predictions.

failing_part: "fitting once at the library's default settings with no search ... predicts at least as well as nested tuning and is better calibrated"
narrowest_regime: None found. Defaults could tie tuning only where the defaults happen to suit the problem, e.g. a strong, simple signal with a large effective size, which is the opposite of n_plan < 300. The real kernel ('tuning parameters chosen on few units are variable') holds, but variance in the chosen settings does not make the untuned defaults better.
reason: At small n the library defaults (XGBoost: eta 0.3, depth 6, min_child_weight 1, 100 rounds; HistGB: lr 0.1, 31 leaves, 100 iterations, no early stopping below 10,000 rows) are under-regularized and overfit, so their probabilities are too extreme. I simulated a binary outcome with nonlinear signal, n=400 (median 136 events) over 22 data sets and n=150 (median 51 events) over 10 data sets, with 3-fold nested tuning over 12 random configurations plus the defaults, and a 20,000-row test set. Calibration slopes were 0.31 (HistGB default) vs 0.88 tuned and 0.24 (XGBoost default) vs 0.96 tuned at n=400, and 0.30/0.22 vs 0.75/0.76 at n=150. Test log loss favored tuning in 100% of data sets, and AUC favored tuning in 80-95%. The cited papers are about penalized regression, not boosting defaults. Van Calster 2020 reports that shrinkage 'improved calibration slopes on average' and Riley 2021 that it is unreliable in individual data sets; neither says unregularized defaults are better calibrated, and Riley recommends larger samples, not untuned fits.

citations.cite: Riley RD et al. Penalization and shrinkage methods produced unreliable clinical prediction models especially when sample size was small. J Clin Epidemiol 2021;132:88-96 (abstract via PubMed 33307188)

Van Calster B, van Smeden M, De Cock B, Steyerberg EW. Regression shrinkage methods for clinical prediction models do not guarantee improved performance: simulation study. Stat Methods Med Res 2020;29(11):3166-3178 (abstract via PubMed 32401702)

Martin GP, Riley RD, Collins GS, Sperrin M. Developing clinical prediction models when adhering to minimum sample size recommendations: the importance of quantifying bootstrap variability in tuning parameters and predictive performance. Stat Methods Med Res 2021;30:2545-2561 (metadata via Crossref)
Probst P, Boulesteix A-L, Bischl B. Tunability: importance of hyperparameters of machine learning algorithms. JMLR 2019;20(53):1-32

bite_note: It sets the tuning plan for every small-data boosted-tree and XGBoost fit to the library defaults, which in simulation produced badly overconfident risks (calibration slope 0.2-0.3) and worse discrimination than nested tuning. It also makes these families look worse in any model comparison.

failing_part: "the NCI measurement-error model is needed and the mean-of-days distribution is ranked lower" in the stated regime ">=2 people with >=2 recalls"
narrowest_regime: Repeat recalls on a replicate subsample large enough to estimate the within-person variance, roughly tens of people (in my simulation the ME estimate clearly wins from about 10-30 repeaters, depending on the within/between variance ratio; Verly 2012 found precision held at replication rates above about 40% of samples of 250+). There, any measurement-error method (NCI, or ISU/MSM, which give similar quantiles in no-covariate models) beats the mean-of-days distribution.
reason: The first half is right. Var(mean of k days) = σ_b² + σ_w²/k > σ_b², so the distribution of single days or two-day means is too wide, and percentiles and cut-off prevalences are biased in both tails, as Tooze 2010 shows. But the regime admits as few as 2 people with a repeat, which leaves the within-person variance with about 2 df. In my simulation (N=500, true prevalence 0.20 below the cut-off), the ME-model prevalence had RMSE 0.096 vs 0.079 for mean-of-days at 2 repeaters (variance ratio 1). σ̂_b² was ≤ 0, a degenerate distribution, in 13-27% of samples, and the ME model did not clearly win until about 10-30 repeaters. 'NCI is needed' is also too specific: Tooze 2010 reports NCI and ISU quantiles as similar, and both superior to individual means.

citations.cite: Tooze JA et al. A mixed-effects model approach for estimating the distribution of usual intake of nutrients: the NCI method. Stat Med 2010;29(27):2857-2868 (abstract via PubMed 20862656)

Tooze JA et al. A new statistical method for estimating the usual intake of episodically consumed foods with application to their distribution. J Am Diet Assoc 2006;106:1575-1587 (metadata via Crossref)

Verly E Jr, Castro MA, Fisberg RM, Marchioni DM. Precision of usual food intake estimates according to the percentage of individuals with a second dietary measurement. J Acad Nutr Diet 2012;112(7):1015-1020 (abstract via PubMed 22889632)

Verly E Jr et al. Performance of statistical methods to correct food intake distribution: comparison between observed and estimated usual intake. Br J Nutr 2016;116(5):897-903 (abstract via PubMed 27523187)

bite_note: With only a handful of repeaters, the recommended NCI distribution can be degenerate or noisier than the labeled mean-of-days one, so ranking NCI first changes the reported prevalence of inadequacy. A minimum replicate count (tens of people) is needed before NCI is ranked first.

failing_part: "averaging k of them cuts within-person variance k-fold" (stated without the independence condition, with 24-hour recalls as the example)
narrowest_regime: Repeats whose within-person deviations are uncorrelated with equal variance and no systematic day effects, e.g. randomly chosen, non-consecutive, day-of-week-balanced recalls. Even then it is exact per unit only for that unit's own k_i; the median k is a summary.
reason: For the mean of k deviations with common variance σ_w² and average pairwise correlation ρ, Var = σ_w²(1+(k−1)ρ)/k. The reduction is k-fold only when ρ = 0, and k/(1+(k−1)ρ) otherwise; with ρ = 0.2 and k = 4 it is 2.5-fold, not 4-fold. Recalls on consecutive days are serially correlated, which is why non-consecutive days are standard, and recall data carry systematic sequence and weekday/weekend effects. NCI-style models add covariates for these, and averaging does not remove them unless they are balanced. As a coach-note rule of thumb the direction and order of magnitude are right.

citations.cite: National Research Council. Nutrient Adequacy: Assessment Using Food Consumption Surveys. National Academy Press, 1986 (non-consecutive days, within-person variance adjustment)
Tooze JA et al. Stat Med 2010;29:2857-2868 (NCI model with covariates; PubMed 20862656)

bite_note: It is an explanatory coach note. It overstates how much a k-day mean shrinks within-person error when days are correlated, but it does not change the aggregation, and the app already ranks the mean-of-days distribution below the measurement-error model. It would bite only if used to compute a corrected variance.

narrowest_regime: The estimate is the mean of the simulated units' final risks r_i, and the simulated units are generated independently given the fitted models: baseline either resampled iid (then the quantity equals the MC SE, a weak bound) or cycled through the observed baseline rows (then strictly conservative). It would fail if the estimate averaged simulated 0/1 events instead of r_i, or if units shared random draws.
reason: The g-formula estimate is mean(r_i). For independently simulated units its Monte Carlo variance is Var(r)/n_sim, and when baseline covariates are fixed at the observed rows the law of total variance gives E[Var(r|L0)]/n_sim ≤ Var(r)/n_sim. In my simulation, sd(r)/√n_sim was 0.99× the true MC SD under iid resampling of the baseline and 1.85-1.89× under cycling. So it is an upper bound (tight in the iid case, up to sd-estimation noise) on MC error only. It does not cover sampling uncertainty, which needs the bootstrap.
bite_note: It only affects the methods text's MC-error figure, which at usual n_sim (thousands) is far below the sampling SE. Calling it a bound rather than an estimate changes no decision.

failing_part: "losing more than 10% of the rows ... is enough to warrant a concern" as a methods threshold, and the kept-vs-dropped comparison of "outcome and predictors" offered as the evidence
narrowest_regime: As a precision-loss and transparency flag, a row-loss threshold is a reasonable convention, and a kept/dropped comparison is a reasonable descriptive. Neither measures complete-case bias. That depends on whether missingness depends on the outcome given the covariates, not on the share dropped.
reason: Complete-case regression is approximately unbiased whenever missingness is independent of the outcome given the model's covariates, at any proportion missing. It can be badly biased below 10% when missingness depends on the outcome (White & Carlin 2010). Madley-Dowd et al. 2019 argue the proportion missing should not guide the MI-vs-CC decision, and that the fraction of missing information is the better guide. The 10% figure is a rule of thumb from practice notes, presented here with no methods derivation. Kept and dropped rows differing in their predictors is expected under covariate-dependent missingness, where CC is fine, so the displayed comparison can signal bias that is not there. The dropped rows' outcome is unobservable when the outcome is what is missing.

citations.cite: White IR, Carlin JB. Bias and efficiency of multiple imputation compared with complete-case analysis for missing covariate values. Stat Med 2010;29(28):2920-2931 (abstract via PubMed 20842622)

Madley-Dowd P, Hughes R, Tilling K, Heron J. The proportion of missing data should not be used to guide decisions on multiple imputation. J Clin Epidemiol 2019;110:63-73 (abstract via PubMed 30878639)

Bennett DA. How can I deal with missing data in my study? Aust N Z J Public Health 2001;25(5):464-469 (exists, PubMed 11688629; the '>10% likely biased' rule commonly attributed to it is not in the abstract)

bite_note: The warning and its kept-vs-dropped table push researchers toward or away from imputation on the share dropped and on covariate imbalance, neither of which identifies CC bias. Under outcome-independent missingness that can trade an unbiased CC estimate for a misspecified MI, and below 10% an outcome-dependent loss goes unflagged.

failing_part: "above 200 exposures (CR2 computed per exposure) the intervals are refused rather than reported as independent", and to a lesser degree the unconditional "would be too narrow"
narrowest_regime: Clustered rows where the exposure and the residual are both positively correlated within unit (unit-level or slowly varying exposures). There, independence intervals are too narrow, and CR2 with Bell-McCaffrey df is a well-supported small-sample choice at any exposure count.
reason: The first two parts hold. The Moulton factor ≈ 1+(m−1)ρ_xρ_e makes naive SEs too small when both intra-cluster correlations are positive, though not when the exposure varies within unit with ρ_x ≤ 0. CR2 with Bell-McCaffrey (Satterthwaite-type) df is the recommended small-cluster correction (Imbens & Kolesár; Pustejovsky & Tipton). The 200-exposure refusal has no methods basis: it is a compute cap, and CR2's cost scales with cluster sizes (Σm_g³ per exposure), not mainly with the exposure count. The choice is not between CR2 and independence: with many clusters CR1/CR0 with t(G−1) is cheap and adequate, so refusing throws away intervals that a valid cluster-robust method could report.

citations.cite: Bell RM, McCaffrey DF. Bias reduction in standard errors for linear regression with multi-stage samples. Survey Methodology 2002;28(2):169-181
Pustejovsky JE, Tipton E. Small-sample methods for cluster-robust variance estimation and hypothesis testing in fixed effects models. J Bus Econ Stat 2018;36:672-683 (metadata via Crossref)
Imbens GW, Kolesár M. Robust standard errors in small samples: some practical advice. NBER WP 18478 (2012); Rev Econ Stat 2016;98(4):701-712 (working paper verified via Crossref)

bite_note: A researcher scanning more than 200 exposures on clustered rows gets no intervals at all, where a cluster-robust CR1 or CR2 interval would have been valid, particularly with many units. Below the cap the CR2/BM choice is sound.

failing_part: "a ratio within 5% of 4.184 x N or of N (N >= 2) could be kJ or an N-day kcal total ... asked together with the fitting readings offered": the 5% match band is half the 0.90-1.10 reconstruction band; and the regime's "at least two macronutrient totals"
narrowest_regime: All three energy macronutrients (protein, carbohydrate, fat, ideally with alcohol) present, with a reconstruction error under about 5%. There the settle rule (kcal only inside 0.90-1.10), the arithmetic (4-day kcal at 4.00 is 4.4% from 4.184) and 'a ratio near 1 never settles the day count' all hold.
reason: The settle rule is safe. Ratio is energy over 4P+4C+9F; every other reading (kJ ≈ 4.18, a 2-day total ≈ 2) lies far outside 0.90-1.10, so it never settles wrongly. The ratio is scale-free in days, so it cannot fix the day count. But the reconstruction error is multiplicative and the same under any unit or day scaling, so a band that tolerates ±10% for kcal must tolerate ±10% around 4.184N and N too. With 5%, a 1-day kJ file whose reconstruction runs 5-7% low (ratio 3.89-3.97) is offered only '4-day kcal', and at 5-10% high it is offered nothing, so the true reading is missing. With only two macronutrients the reconstruction is incomplete: a 1-day kcal file with protein and fat only reads about 2.0 and is offered a spurious '2-day kcal total'.

citations.cite: Merrill AL, Watt BK. Energy Value of Foods: Basis and Derivation. USDA Agriculture Handbook No. 74, 1955/1973 (Atwater general factors 4/4/9/7 kcal/g)

bite_note: The unit question is asked, but the readings offered can leave out the true unit (kJ) or propose a wrong day count. If the researcher picks from them, every energy-based screen and energy adjustment is off by a factor of 4.184 or of N.

failing_part: "one input's share is said to be unstable when the reseeds' rank correlation is under 0.7"
narrowest_regime: The first two parts hold for any fitted model. SHAP and ALE describe the model's input-output map, not interventions (Molnar et al. 2022), and within a group of correlated inputs the split of credit depends on the model's arbitrary choice among near-substitutes and on the SHAP value function, while the group total is the stable quantity. A reseed-agreement check is reasonable as a stability heuristic, with the cut-off treated as a convention.
reason: The causal disclaimer and the arbitrariness of within-group credit are sound and match the cited pitfalls literature. The 0.7 cut-off appears in none of the cited sources (Lundberg & Lee define SHAP, Apley & Zhu define ALE, Molnar et al. list pitfalls), and nothing derives it, so it is a convention presented as sourced. A rank correlation across reseeds is also a property of the whole ranking of inputs, not of one input's share. A single input's instability needs a per-input measure, such as the spread of its share or rank across reseeds.

citations.cite: Lundberg SM, Lee S-I. A unified approach to interpreting model predictions. NeurIPS 2017 (30):4765-4774
Apley DW, Zhu J. Visualizing the effects of predictor variables in black box supervised learning models. JRSS-B 2020;82(4):1059-1086 (metadata via Crossref)
Molnar C et al. General pitfalls of model-agnostic interpretation methods for machine learning models. In: xxAI - Beyond Explainable AI, LNCS 13200, 2022:39-68 (metadata via Crossref)

bite_note: The cut-off decides which drivers are shown as unstable in the 'what drives it' reading; a different threshold, or a per-input measure, would relabel inputs. The causal disclaimer, which carries most of the bite, is correct.

narrowest_regime: Holds as a design-calibrated wording convention. Unqualified causal wording is warranted only for the randomized comparison of a trial; per-protocol or non-randomized exposures within a trial need the middle tier, and 'only for trials' is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. The app-internal gate 'no standing question points elsewhere' is an engineering condition I could not evaluate.
reason: The three tiers track what each design identifies. Randomization identifies the effect of assignment without untestable exchangeability assumptions. Observational estimates are causal only under named assumptions (exchangeability, positivity, consistency), which is what the 'estimated effect, its assumptions named' tier says, matching Hernán 2018's argument for stating the causal aim explicitly rather than hiding it behind 'association'. An association floor for observational designs matches JAMA's 'Use of Causal Language' reporting requirement. Model explanations (SHAP, ALE, importance) describe the fitted function and are not interventional effects (Molnar et al. 2022). Withholding the middle tier when a stated assumption is refuted is the right direction. Non-refutation is weak evidence, since exchangeability is untestable, but the tier already names the assumptions as assumptions.

citations.cite: Hernán MA. The C-word: scientific euphemisms do not improve causal inference from observational data. Am J Public Health 2018;108(5):616-619 (abstract via PubMed 29565659)
JAMA Instructions for Authors, 'Use of Causal Language' (section heading confirmed on jamanetwork.com; exact wording restricting causal terms to RCTs not retrieved)
Molnar C et al. General pitfalls of model-agnostic interpretation methods for machine learning models. LNCS 13200, 2022:39-68 (metadata via Crossref)

bite_note: It sets the drafted Results wording and flags stronger user wording. Compared with letting any design claim effects, it prevents causal overstatement in observational results and model-explanation sections.
